question: what is the ceiling on what the delta route could save, and does it pay for itself

corpus.fact_cache: warm -- this is the cost of reindexing after an edit, not a cold build
corpus.languages: go, typescript and rust -- all three loaded, which the first run of this benchmark did not achieve

skips: staging (writing the canonical graph from scratch)

projection.note: the mutation itself is excluded: it scales with the edit, and CanonicalTableCounts reading all eighteen relationship tables in 0.030 s bounds per-table work on this database at about 2 ms

limitations: the delta route has no production caller, so its cost is projected from the steps applyDeltaRoute provably runs, never measured end to end
ApplyCanonicalDelta is not timed here: building a workspace-scale delta needs real loader output for workspace, and the fixed costs already decide the question
one corpus, one machine, one warm cache; a cold cache moves the language engines from 0.57 s to minutes and makes every ratio here look better than it is
the full pass numbers come from one run with per-event timestamps, not from a distribution
the first run of this benchmark measured a corpus with no Rust in it, because cargo was missing from the harness PATH; the figures here replace those and the correction block records what moved

correction.what: the first run of this benchmark indexed workspace without Rust
correction.why: the harness PATH carried CARGO_HOME but not cargo itself, so rust-analyzer refused both Cargo workspaces and the pass published the rest -- which kivgraph reported as rust_workspaces_not_loaded=2 in both its JSON and its human output, and the harness ignored
correction.effect_on_the_conclusion: none in direction. Rust facts are cached like every other language, so a warm pass grows by 0.861 s and every phase share stays within a point: staging is 37.1 % where it was 38.5 %, and it remains the only step a delta avoids
